content: 1. The quality of evidence supporting the recommendation for psychological interventions for bereaved adults is considered very low. However, the general principles of care outlined in the WHO (2010) mhGAP Intervention Guide should be taken into account. These principles emphasize effective communication, mobilizing and providing social support, and addressing overall well-being. Additionally, the principles of psychological first aid should be applied. Participation in culturally appropriate mourning practices is encouraged. 2. Benzodiazepines should not be offered to bereaved children and adolescents who do not meet the criteria for a mental disorder. This recommendation is strong, but the quality of evidence supporting it is very low. As with bereaved adults, the general principles of care from the WHO (2010) mhGAP Intervention Guide should be considered, including communication, social support, and attention to well-being. Psychological first aid principles should also be applied. Culturally appropriate mourning practices should be encouraged. In cases where a child has lost a primary caregiver, issues of protection and continued supportive caregiving, including socio-emotional support, must be addressed. 3. The WHO plans to disseminate, adapt, and implement these recommendations through the development of an mhGAP clinical module focused on managing stress-related disorders and problems in adults, adolescents, and children. This module will be distributed widely via WHO regional and country offices, collaborating centers, professional organizations, and partner agencies. It will also be promoted as a WHO-UNHCR tool for humanitarian work. Evidence profiles will be uploaded to the WHO mhGAP Evidence Resource Centre, and an article will be submitted to a public health journal to share the guidelines and their development process. 4. The recommendations will be adapted for field use by creating appropriate training materials in consultation with regional, national, and local stakeholders. Adaptation will include translation into relevant languages and ensuring that interventions are culturally acceptable and suitable for local health systems. Monitoring and evaluation tools will be developed to assess the implementation of the mhGAP Intervention Guide and the stress-related module. These tools will include input, process, output, and outcome measures. 5. The mhGAP program has successfully attracted significant funding for global mental health research from organizations such as the UK Department for International Development (DFID), the US National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH), the European Commission (EC), and Grand Challenges Canada. These funds have primarily supported university partners in studying the impact of applying mhGAP guidelines, including strengthening implementation and dissemination science. 6. In some cases, the Guideline Development Group (GDG) determined that there was insufficient evidence to make recommendations. In such instances, the quality of evidence was summarized as very low. New research is needed to address all scoping questions with low or very low-quality evidence. The recommendations and evidence base should be reviewed within five years, before 2018. 7. Acute traumatic stress symptoms, such as intrusion, avoidance, hyperarousal, hyperventilation, dissociation, insomnia, and bedwetting (in children), are common in the aftermath of potentially traumatic events. These symptoms can significantly impair daily functioning within the first month after the event. Early psychological interventions for adults with acute traumatic stress symptoms should be evaluated for their effectiveness in reducing symptoms, improving functioning and quality of life, and minimizing adverse effects.
